REMARKS
Applicant has carefully reviewed the non-final Office Action mailed on June 7, 2023 and offers the following remarks to accompany the above amendments.
Summary of Remarks

With respect to the rejected claims (and as indicated in the Office Action), the cited art fails to disclose or suggest a wearable fetal health monitoring device for determining a heath condition of a fetus based on biosignals of an expecting mother and the fetus as recited in claim 1 that includes a ferroelectric nanogenerator sensor that detects abdominal pressure waves.
Status of the Claims
Claims 1-20 were previous pending. Claims 1, 9, and 17 are amended herein. Claim 15 is canceled herein. Claim 21 is added herein. As such, claims 1-14 and 16-21 remain pending.
Drawings
The drawings are objected to because FIGS. 1A, 1B, 2, 3A, 3C, 3D, 5, and 6 are difficult to read. Applicant has provided replacement sheets for FIGS. 1A, 1B, 2, 3A, 3C. 3D, 5, and 6 herein.
Accordingly, it is respectfully submitted that the objection to the drawings be withdrawn.
Claim Objections
Claim 17 is objected to because informalities: Applicant has amended claim 17 to delete lines 18-25 after the period as indicated by the Office Action.
Accordingly, it is respectfully submitted that the objection to claim 17 be withdrawn.

Claim 1, 12, and 17 stand rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112 as failing to comply with the written description requirement. The Office Action contends the subject matter was not described in the specification in such a way as to reasonably convey to a person of ordinary skill in the art had possession of the claimed invention.

Regarding claims 1 and 17, the Office Action further identifies the limitation reciting "identify a noise correction value" based on comparing "the first mHR value with the second mHR value." Applicant respectfully traverses the rejection. Applicant contends that a person of ordinary skill in the art would be in possession of knowledge of how to compare the first mHR value with the second mHR value to identify a noise correction value. Further in the rejection 35 USC § 103 of the above limitation, the Office Action contents that Holt (WO 2019133926 filed on 12/28/18) teaches the above limitation in paragraph [00075] as follows:
In some embodiments, execution of step 415 may include

processing one or more of the signals received in step 305 with a secondary signal received in step 410. For example, if the secondary signal is a maternal heartrate signal (as may be received from, for example, ECG device 170), then the maternal heartrate signal may be used to determine which portions of the signals received in step 305 are contributed by the pregnant mammal. These portions may then be subtracted and/or divided from the signals received in step 305 to remove maternal contributions to the signals received in step 305. Additionally, or alternatively, if the secondary signal is a fetal heartrate signal, then the fetal heartrate signal may be used to determine which portions of the

signals received in step 305 are contributed by the fetus because, for example, the oxygenation level of the fetus may fluctuate in a manner that corresponds to its pulse or heartrate. These portions of the signals received in step 305 may then be amplified by, for example, multiplying them by the fetal signal produced by subtracting portions of the maternal contributions from the signals received in step 305 and/or subtraction of portions of the signals received in step 305 that are not
contributed by the fetus.
Further in the rejection under 35 USC § 103 of the above limitation, the Office Action contents that Bureev (RU 2656518 filed on 3/6/14) teaches the above limitation in claim 1 as follows:

mother in the antenatal period of pregnancy, including recording heart sounds of the fetus and the expectant mother using sensors placed on the mother's abdomen, filtering, transmitting, processing, storing in a database and evaluating the data obtained with reference samples, characterized the fact that in addition to the continuous flow of signals of the heart sounds of the mother, the moment of absence of the heart tone of the mother is determined, and at this time the level of external noise is measured, the ratio of the amplitudes mentioned of weak signals and calculate the attenuation coefficient of external noise and interference, by which the signals of external noise are multiplied before summing with the signals of the heart sounds of the mother, and a similar procedure is performed for the signals of the heart sounds of the fetus
and external noise to proportionally attenuate the external noise and
interference before subtracting from the recorded tones fetal heart.

The Office Action further cites that it would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art to combine the references of Holt and Bureev to teach the limitations of claims 1 and 17 including the limitation of comparing the first mHR value with the second mHR value to identify a noise correction value. As such, the Applicant believes the above limitation was described in the specification in such a way as to reasonably convey to a person of ordinary skill in the art how to practice the claimed invention.

Regarding claim 12, the Office Action further identifies the limitation reciting "deconvolute the abdominal acoustic signal" based on "using at least one of the first mHR value and the second mHR value" Applicant respectfully traverses the rejection. Applicant contends that a person of ordinary skill in the art would be in possession of knowledge of how to deconvolute the abdominal acoustic signal using at least one of the first mHR value and the second mHR value. Further in the rejection 35 USC § 103 of the above limitation, the Office Action contents that Chen (WO 2018148251 filed on 2/7/18) teaches the above limitation in paragraphs [0047], [00098], and [0099] as follows:
[0047] A methodology is disclosed that enables calculation of the

systolic and diastolic blood pressures continuously in a non-invasive manner, based on the heart sounds measured from the chest of a human being. To this end, first and second heart sounds, known as Si and S2, are

separated from directly measured heart sound signals. Next, individual characteristics of Si and S2 are identified and correlated to systolic and diastolic blood pressures. As known, material properties of a human being are inhomogeneous, changing from one organ to another, and the speed at which the heart sound signals propagate inside a human body cannot always be determined precisely. Moreover, the exact locations from which the heart sounds are originated are estimated. As such, the disclosed method is semi-empirical. Yet, validation results have demonstrated that this semi-empirical computer model can produce robust and accurate calculations of the systolic and diastolic blood
pressures.
[0098] The following portion of the disclosure presents a

theoretical foundation for the disclosed methodology that enables the prediction of blood pressures based on the heart sounds measured directly on the chest of a patient. One aspect of this methodology is the separation of heart sounds into first heart sound and second heart sound, from which components attributable to four heart valves, i.e.: mitral; tricuspid; aortic; and pulmonary valve-closure sounds are separated. Because human physiology and anatomy can vary among people and are unknown a priori, such separation is called blind source separation. Moreover, the sources locations, their surroundings and boundary conditions are unspecified. Consequently, it is difficult to obtain an exact separation of signals. To circumvent this difficulty, the point source separation method is extended in this disclosure to an inhomogeneous fluid medium, and further combined with iteration schemes to search for approximate source locations and signal propagation speed. Once these are accomplished, the signals emitted
from individual sources are separated by deconvoluting mixed signals
with respect to the identified sources.
[0099] Blind Source Separation (BSS) aims at separating
individual signals from a set of mixed data collected by multiple sensors.

Applications of BSS have been found in almost all fields including analyzing bio-medical signals, speeches, machine health monitoring, radio communications, and others. In particular, in bio-acoustical fields, BSS have been used to improve speech recognition in bilateral cochlear implant patients, to analyze functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data, electroencephalography (EEG) signals, etc. In analyzing acoustic signals, locating and separating noise sources via multi-channel microphones is an effective approach for both airborne and structural- born noise problems. BSS also enables one to extract target vibration signals generated by a specific mechanical machine from directly measured data that have been contaminated by interfering signals emitted from other machines, which can be very helpful for machine
health monitoring and diagnosis.

The Office Action further cites that it would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art to combine Chen with the other cited references to teach the limitation of claims 1 and 12 including the limitation of "deconvoluting the abdominal acoustic signal using at least one of the first mHR value and the second mHR value." As such, the Applicant believes the above limitation was described in the specification in such a way as to reasonably convey to a person of ordinary skill in the art how to practice the claimed invention.
Accordingly, it is respectfully submitted that the rejection of claims 1, 12, and 17 under 35 USC § 112 be withdrawn.

Claims 1-20 stand rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 because the claimed invention is directed to a judicial exception (i.e., a law of nature, a natural phenomenon, or an abstract idea) without significantly more. The Office Action further contends claims 1-20 are directed toward an abstract idea related to certain methods of organizing human activity such as commercial or legal interactions including advertising, marketing or sales activities or behaviors, or business relations and fail to pass Step 2A - Prong 1 of the Alice/Mayo analysis. Additionally, the Office Action contends claims 1-20 are not integrated into a practical application and fail to pass Step 2A - Prong 2 of the Alice/Mayo analysis. Finally, the Office Action contends claims 1-20 do not include additional elements that are sufficient to amount to significantly more than the judicial exception and fail to pass Step 2B of the Alice/Mayo analysis.

The following remarks will address claims 1-20 in regard to Step 2A - Prong 2 and Step 2B of the Alice/Mayo analysis.
Updates to the Federal Register / Vol 84. No. 4 on Monday, January 7, 2019 titled "2019 Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidance" recites the following regarding Step 2A - Prong 2:

Prong Two represents a change from prior guidance. The analysis under Prong Two is the same for all claims reciting a judicial exception, whether the exception is an abstract idea, a law of nature, or a natural
phenomenon.

In the context of revised Step 2A, the following exemplary considerations are indicative that an additional element (or combination of elements) [24] may have integrated the exception into a practical
application:
e An additional element reflects an improvement in the
functioning of a computer, or an improvement to other technology
or technical field.
Additionally, slide 19 of the 2019 PEG -Advanced Module dated January 2019 identifies Step 2A as a two prong inquiry with updated guidance to Step 2A-Prong 2 as follows:
o Revised Step 2A: Prong Two
" New procedure not found in prior guidance:
e Identifying whether there are any additional elements recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception(s), and
e Evaluating those additional elements to determine whether they integrate the exception into a practical application of the exception. " "Integration into a practical application"

e Requires an additional element or a combination of additional elements in the claim to apply, rely on, or use the judicial exception in a manner that imposes a meaningful limit on the judicial exception, such that the claim is more than a drafting effort designed to monopolize the exception.
e Uses the considerations laid out by the Supreme Court and the Federal Circuit to evaluate whether the judicial exception is integrated into a practical application.
Further, page 11 of the USPTO Memorandum titled "October 2019 Update: Subject Matter Eligibility" recites the following regarding Step 2B -Prong 2:
"For example, if the additional limitations reflect an improvement in the functioning of a computer, or an improvement to another technology or
technical field, the claim integrates the judicial exception into a practical application and thus imposes a meaningful limit on the judicial exception.
No further analysis is required. The claim is eligible at Step 2A."

Amended claim 1 recites additional limitations that reflect an improvement of a technical field (e.g., determining a heath condition of a fetus based on biosignals of an expecting mother and the fetus). More specifically, amended claim 1 recites a wearable fetal health monitoring device including additional limitations as follows:
a microcontroller configured to:
generate a maternal phonocardiogram (mPCG) value from the
abdominal acoustic signal;
calculate a first maternal heart rate (mHR) value from the mPCG
value;
calculate a second mHR value from the mPPG value;
compare the first mHR value with the second mHR value to identify
a noise correction value; and
apply the identified noise correction value to the mPCG value to
extract a fetal phonocardiogram (fPCG) value.

In addition to the microcontroller of the wearable fetal health monitoring device, the claim is further limited by a microelectromechanical system (MEMS) accelerometer configured to convert an acoustic wave sensed in an abdominal region into an abdominal acoustic signal, a pulse oximeter configured to generate a maternal photoplethysmogram (mPPG) value from a pulse sensed in the abdominal region; and a ferroelectric nanogenerator sensor configured to detect abdominal pressure waves;

The microcontroller works in concert with the microelectromechanical system (MEMS) accelerometer; the pulse oximeter, and the ferroelectric nanogenerator sensor to extract a fetal phonocardiogram (fPCG) value. As such, determining a heath condition of a fetus based on biosignals of an expecting mother and the fetus is improved.

A person of ordinary skill in the art would understand that such a method must be implemented on a computing device and to be practical to extract a fetal phonocardiogram (fPCG) value between heartbeats of the expecting mother and the fetus. Accordingly, amended claim 1 recites a practical application. As such for the reasons above, amended claim 1 passes Step 2A Prong Two of the Alice/Mayo analysis.

In the event the Patent Office believes amended claim 1 is still directed at a judicial exception that is not integrated into a practical application and fails to pass Step 2A of the Alice/Mayo analysis, a further analysis of amended claim 13 against Step 2B follows.

The following paragraph and reference are recited on page 51 in the updates to the Federal Register /Vol 84. No. 4 on Monday, January 7, 2019 titled "2019 Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidance":

Finally, if further analysis at Step 2B is needed (for example to determine whether the claim merely recites well-understood, routine, conventional activity), this 2019 Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidance explains that the examiner or administrative patent judge will proceed in
accordance with existing USPTO guidance as modified in April 2018.[6]
6. USPTO Memorandum of April 19, 2018, "Changes in Examination Procedure Pertaining to Subject Matter Eligibility, Recent Subject Matter
Eligibility Decision (Berkheimer v. HP, Inc.)" (Apr. 19, 2018),

The above USPTO Memorandum recites in Section III updated requirements for a Step 2B analysis of Alice/Mayo. As Applicant understands this guidance, the Examiner must support a 101 rejection using at least one of the following four points of the Memorandum to determine that the combination of elements are well-understood, routine or conventional in nature:
1. A citation to an express statement in the specification or to a statement
made by an applicant during prosecution that demonstrates the well-
understood, routine, conventional nature of the additional element(s).

A specification demonstrates the well-understood, routine, conventional nature of additional elements when it describes the additional elements as well-understood or routine or conventional (or an equivalent term), as a commercially available product, or in a manner that indicates that the additional elements are sufficiently well-known that the specification does not need to describe the particulars of such additional elements to satisfy 35 U.S.C. @ 112(a). A finding that an element is well-understood, routine, or conventional cannot be based only on the fact that the specification is silent with
respect to describing such element.
2. A citation to one or more of the court decisions discussed in MPEP @
2106.05(d)(II) as noting the well-understood, routine, conventional
nature of the additional element(s).
3. A citation to a publication that demonstrates the well-understood,

routine, conventional nature of the additional element(s). An appropriate publication could include a book, manual, review article, or other source that describes the state of the art and discusses what is well-known and in common use in the relevant industry. It does not include all items that might otherwise qualify as a "printed publication" as used in 35 U.S.C. @ 102.3. Whether something is disclosed in a document that is considered a "printed publication"

under 3 5 U.S. C @ 102 is a distinct inquiry from whether something is well-known, routine, conventional activity. A document may be a printed publication but still fail to establish that something it describes is well-understood, routine, conventional activity. See Exergen Corp., 2018 WL 1193529, at *4 (the single copy of a thesis written in German and located in a German university library considered to be a "printed

publication" in Hall "would not suffice to establish that something is 'well-understood, routine, and conventional activity previously engaged in by scientists who work in the field"'). The nature of the publication and the description of the additional elements in the publication would need to demonstrate that the additional elements are widely prevalent or in common use in the relevant field, comparable to the types of activity or elements that are so well-known that they do not need to be described in detail in a patent application to satisfy 35 U.S.C. @ 112(a). For example, while U.S. patents and published applications are publications, merely finding the additional element in a single patent or published application would not be sufficient to demonstrate that the additional element is well- understood, routine, conventional, unless the patent or published application demonstrates that the additional element are widely
prevalent or in common use in the relevant field.
4. A statement that the examiner is taking official notice of the well- understood, routine, conventional nature of the additional element(s).

This option should be used only when the examiner is certain, based upon his or her personal knowledge, that the additional element(s) represents well-understood, routine, conventional activity engaged in by those in the relevant art, in that the additional elements are widely prevalent or in common use in the relevant field, comparable to the types of activity or elements that are so well-known that they do not need to be described in detail in a patent application to satisfy 35 U.S.C. @ 112(a). Procedures for taking official notice and addressing an applicant's challenge to official notice are discussed in MPEP @

Taking into account the above guidance, it is clear that the additional elements recited in the present claims amount to significantly more than the judicial exception and therefor are patent-eligible subject matter because the additional elements is not well- understood, routine, or conventional in nature as required by at least one of the above four points of the Memorandum.

Regarding point 1 of the Memorandum, nowhere has Applicant cited in the Specification, or during prosecution that the above additional elements would be well- understood, routine, or conventional in nature to a person of ordinary skill in the art at the priority date of the application.

Regarding point 2 of the Memorandum, Applicant is unaware of any court decisions discussed in MPEP § 2106.05(d)(II) as noting a well-understood, routine, or conventional in nature the above additional elements.

Regarding point 3 of the Memorandum, the Office Action fails to cite any references that disclose the above additional elements as well-understood, routine, or conventional in nature. Specifically, the limitation of originally filed claim 15 now incorporated into amended claim 1.
Regarding point 4 of the Memorandum, the Examiner has not taken official notice in the Office Action that the above additional elements are well-understood, routine, or conventional in nature.
As such, amended claim 1 in addition to passing Step 2A also passes Step 2B of the Alice/Mayo analysis.
